# RAG, agents, and where they break {#sec-ch06}

If you ask an LLM what your company's backup account is allowed to do, it will give a confident and well-written answer that is completely made up. It has never seen your company's documents. So we give it the right documents to read, and then we give it tools so it can take actions. This is where most of today's AI excitement is, and also where many hidden failures happen. As you read, notice one pattern: almost every weak point is a small decision.

::: {.goals}
- Understand RAG, and why the search step is the weak link.
- See that most of an agent's work is making decisions.
- Learn how one planted sentence can mislead a model, and how to stop it.
:::

## Giving the model the right page

![Retrieval-augmented generation. The question goes to a search step first, which pulls the most relevant chunks from your documents. The LLM sees the question plus those chunks, and answers from them, ideally citing which one it used.](/figures/ch12/pipeline.pdf){#fig-pipeline}

**Retrieval-augmented generation**, or **RAG**, works in three steps. First, search your documents for the passages most related to the question. Second, add those passages to the question. Third, ask the LLM to answer using them (@fig-pipeline) [@lewis2020]. In our example, with a set of company policies mixed with many similar-looking but useless documents, the search found the correct passage first {{< num ch12 recall.char.0 pct >}} of the time.

The most important part of RAG is not the LLM; it is the search. If the correct passage is not found, the LLM simply builds the most likely-sounding answer from whatever it has. The answer will look fluent, will even mention a source, and will still be wrong.

::: {.keyidea}
**An AI that reads your documents is only as good as its search.** If the search finds the wrong page, the LLM still writes a confident, fluent answer, and it is wrong. Test the search first.
:::

Some questions have no answer in the documents at all. A good system should then say "I don't know". A simple signal is how closely the *best* passage matches the question.

![The similarity of the best-matching chunk, for questions the knowledge base can answer (green, solid bars) and questions it can't (red, striped outline). They overlap, but not much. Below a threshold, the system should decline to answer.](/figures/ch12/abstain.pdf){#fig-abstain}

With a threshold on this match score, the system answered {{< num ch12 answered_share pct >}} of the questions that had answers, and only {{< num ch12 unans_answered pct >}} of those that did not (@fig-abstain). So even a system built for writing depends on a small yes-or-no decision with a threshold.

## A model in a loop: agents

An **agent** is a model working in a loop with tools: it looks at the situation, decides what to do, does it, and looks again. When people say an agent "uses a tool", the model does not press any button itself. It only writes which tool it wants and with what inputs [@yao2023]. Your program checks this request and runs it. So each tool request is really a choice from a fixed list.

![What the agent spent its steps on, averaged over 300 alerts. Small typed decisions dominate. Free text, the thing LLMs are famous for, is a small minority of the work.](/figures/ch13/census.pdf){#fig-census}

Consider an example security agent. For each alert, it decides which evidence to collect, whether it has enough, and the final verdict, and then it acts. When we count its steps, decisions are {{< num ch13 share_decide pct >}} of all steps and writing is only {{< num ch13 share_generate pct >}} (@fig-census). Count the steps of any agent, and you will usually find the same pattern.

::: {.keyidea}
**Most of an AI agent's work is small decisions, not writing.** Which tool to use? Is this enough information? Is this action safe? If these small choices are wrong, the whole agent fails.
:::

## Small mistakes multiply

If each step is correct 95% of the time, a task with ten steps succeeds only 0.95 × 0.95 × … ten times, which is about {{< num ch13 compound_95_10 pct >}}. With twenty steps, it is about {{< num ch13 compound_95_20 pct >}}.

![The chance that every step of a task goes right, for different per-step reliabilities. Small per-step error rates become large task failure rates as the number of steps grows.](/figures/ch13/compound.pdf){#fig-compound}

This is why agents look great in demos, which are short and easy, but fail in real work, which is long and messy (@fig-compound). Since decisions are most of the steps, they carry most of the risk. If each decision comes with a trusted probability, an unsure step can be stopped and sent for checking.

## When the input itself lies

Agents read text written by other people: emails, tickets, web pages. An attacker can hide instructions or false statements in that text. This is called **prompt injection** [@greshake2023]. It is not only a problem for LLMs; any model that reads text written by an attacker can be misled.

![How likely the decision model thinks each real threat is, reading the alert text as written (black, solid line) and with one planted sentence (red, dashed line). The sentence pulls many real threats below the auto-close threshold. When the same fact comes from a trusted system instead (green, dotted fill), the planted sentence does nothing.](/figures/ch14/injection.pdf){#fig-injection}

For example, some alerts contain the line "Matches approved IT tooling (change ticket on file)", which strongly suggests the alert is harmless. Suppose an attacker adds this line inside a file name. In our example, the share of real attacks that would be closed without anyone checking jumps from {{< num ch14 inj_act_before pct >}} to {{< num ch14 inj_act_after pct >}} (@fig-injection). The fix is in the design, not in a smarter model: ask the company's ticket system directly whether such a ticket exists, and pass that answer separately, where the attacker cannot write. Then only {{< num ch14 inj_act_trusted pct >}} are closed.

::: {.keyidea}
**Do not let an attacker write the facts that make something look safe.** If an email itself says "approved by IT", anyone could have typed that. Check such facts in your own trusted systems instead.
:::

## The decision layer

Almost every protection in this chapter is the same thing: a check that becomes a decision, with a threshold based on the cost of mistakes. Put all of them together and you get a **decision layer** between what an agent wants to do and what actually happens.

![A decision layer between what an agent proposes and what actually happens: schema and allow-list checks, a typed decision with a calibrated probability, a threshold from costs, a budget and trusted facts, then one of three doors.](/figures/ch14/defences.pdf){#fig-defences}

The decision layer checks each proposed action against what is allowed, asks clear questions, uses thresholds based on costs, takes risky facts only from trusted systems, and sends each case through one of the three doors: act, review or escalate (@fig-defences). If anything fails, such as a timeout or an unreadable answer, the case goes to a person. None of this needs a smarter model. It needs decisions that are fast, cheap and calibrated.

::: {.threshold}
An agent can close an alert, add a note, block a sender's website, or disconnect a laptop from the network. Which actions can it do automatically when confident, and which should always need a person?

(Closing an alert and adding a note are cheap and can be undone, so they can be automatic with a good threshold. Blocking a website can be undone but may hurt business, so use a stricter threshold and a list of partners it must never block. Disconnecting a laptop stops someone's work and may destroy evidence, so a person should decide.)
:::

1. A company says its agent gets 90% of steps right, and a normal task has fifteen steps. What success rate would you expect for a full task?
